title: Last, and first
hook: heaven and earth last because they don't live for themselves; the sage puts himself last (Tao Te Ching 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the valley spirit, and your line was the valley: stay low, and let things arrive. Did you get a chance? Chapter seven takes the low place and turns it into a question of who goes first. Day one thousand sixty-nine.

A four-way stop, late afternoon. Two cars arrive at the same moment. Both drivers hesitate. One waves: go ahead. The other waves back: no, you. A little dance of hands through windshields, and then, finally, somebody goes, and both drivers are smiling as they pull away. Nobody lost anything. A few seconds, at most. And for a moment, two strangers who'll never meet were on the same side. Chapter seven of the Tao Te Ching is about the strange strength of going last, and it starts with the sky and the ground.
screen: `TWO CARS, ONE MOMENT.` → `GO AHEAD. NO, YOU.` → `NOBODY LOST ANYTHING.`

segments.voice: First, heaven and earth last. Legge's translation opens: "Heaven is long-enduring and earth continues long." Why? The chapter answers: because they don't live for themselves. The sky doesn't hoard its rain. The ground doesn't keep its harvest. They give everything away, and they go on and on. Second, the sage puts himself last. Then the chapter turns to people. In Legge's words, "the sage puts his own person last, and yet it is found in the foremost place." He treats his own self as if it were outside him, the chapter says, and yet his self is kept safe. Not grasping, and somehow not lost. Third, not a trick for getting ahead. The chapter ends with a question: isn't it because the sage has no private aims that his aims are fulfilled? Readers take this two ways. Some hear a kind of strategy: hold back, and you'll end up ahead. Others say that if you go last in order to be first, you've already missed it, because the point was not to be living for yourself at all. The chapter doesn't settle it. It just sets the paradox down and leaves. Fourth, an echo in Matthew. The Gospel of Matthew has its own saying, at the end of a parable where workers hired at the last hour are paid first. In the King James words: "So the last shall be first, and the first last." The parable keeps its own meaning, and the chapter keeps its own. What they share is an upside-down order.
screen: `HEAVEN AND EARTH LAST.` · `THE SAGE PUTS HIMSELF LAST.` · `NOT A TRICK FOR GETTING AHEAD.` · `AN ECHO IN MATTHEW.` · then, large: `LAST, AND FIRST.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to let someone go first, and the sit is where you get ready for it. Settle, and breathe. Picture the places today where there will be a small line: a doorway, a coffee counter, a merge onto the highway, a turn to talk in a meeting. Choose one, and see yourself stepping back there, with a small gesture: go ahead. Notice what that costs, which is probably very little. Breathe into the space it leaves. If you pray, you can offer that small step back. If you don't, just rehearse the gesture. The bell holds the time.
Last. In chapter seven, heaven and earth last because they don't live for themselves, and the sage who puts himself last is found in front. Today's word.
Your line: last, and first. At the moment you picked, step back and let someone go first, and don't keep count of it afterward. Day one thousand sixty-nine.

howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching take chapter seven into small daily choices, stepping back in lines, conversations and traffic, as a way of not living only for themselves.
